scholarly_argument_wells_divine_human_ag.page: 297-301 (Chapter 11: Conclusions, sec. 11.2.2: Human Obedience and Divine Agency)
scholarly_argument_wells_divine_human_ag.chapter: Chapter 11, sec. 11.2.2.1: Human and Divine Agency in Dynamic Integration
scholarly_argument_wells_divine_human_ag.quote_verbatim: But in Paul's mind the agency of the Spirit reinforces rather than negates human responsibility, because the two agents exist in an essentially non-contrastive relationship: they neither relate in inverse proportion, nor in simple one-plus-one addition. They coinhere, yet the basic integrity of each remains. ... Rather than conceiving divine and human agency as 'one or the other' or 'one plus the other', 'one beside the other', or 'one becoming the other', for Paul human works are taken up and established in the divine work: 'one in the other'.
scholarly_argument_wells_divine_human_ag.context: Wells' central formulation of the dynamic-integration / coinherence thesis: divine and human agencies are non-contrastive but coinhere; human agency is established by divine agency, never autonomous.

scholarly_argument_wells_pauline_anthrop.pdf_source: /Users/romaingirardi/Desktop/DOCTORAT/Doctorat SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/NTSupp 157 Kyle B. Wells-Grace and Agency in Paul and Second Temple Judaism_ Interpreting the Transformation of the Heart-Brill Academic Publishers (2014).md
scholarly_argument_wells_pauline_anthrop.page: 297 (Chapter 11, sec. 11.2.1: Moral Competence and Human Transformation)
scholarly_argument_wells_pauline_anthrop.quote_verbatim: The newly created moral agent is constituted as such precisely as she stands in ongoing relation to God through the reception of his gift (cf. Gal 3:2-5); and, for this very reason, the reconstituted agent can never and will never be an autonomous agent.
scholarly_argument_wells_pauline_anthrop.context: Wells' definitive anti-libertarian statement for Paul: the reconstituted moral agent is competent but never autonomous; the term autexousios does not appear in the volume. Wells also cites Schnelle (Wells_2014.md:277-278): 'The question of human free will represents a central problem of Pauline theology and anthropology' — but Wells' positive answer is Spirit-dependent agency, not libertarian free will.

scholarly_argument_wells_pauline_integra.pdf_source: /Users/romaingirardi/Desktop/DOCTORAT/Doctorat SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/NTSupp 157 Kyle B. Wells-Grace and Agency in Paul and Second Temple Judaism_ Interpreting the Transformation of the Heart-Brill Academic Publishers (2014).md
scholarly_argument_wells_pauline_integra.page: 295-296 (Chapter 11, sec. 11.2: Pauline Integration of Grace and Agency); 300-301
scholarly_argument_wells_pauline_integra.quote_verbatim: Our investigation into Paul's reading of Scripture has brought issues regarding the relationship between grace and obedience into clearer focus. Any adequate analysis of how Paul integrates these two fundamental elements must take into consideration his conceptions of moral competence, human transformation, and the multiplex way in which he structures divine and human agency. ... On Paul's count, eschatological agents do not become less, but more fully human as God acts, and are constituted as agents precisely as they function as God's agency.
scholarly_argument_wells_pauline_integra.context: Wells' overall integration thesis: heart-transformation reconstitutes the moral agent, and grace and human agency are integrated rather than opposed.

scholarly_argument_wells_deuteronomy_and.pdf_source: /Users/romaingirardi/Desktop/DOCTORAT/Doctorat SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/NTSupp 157 Kyle B. Wells-Grace and Agency in Paul and Second Temple Judaism_ Interpreting the Transformation of the Heart-Brill Academic Publishers (2014).md
scholarly_argument_wells_deuteronomy_and.chapter: Chapter 2: Deuteronomy 30 — God and Israel in the Drama of Restoration
scholarly_argument_wells_deuteronomy_and.quote_verbatim: Thus far it has been argued that Paul reads Deuteronomy 30:1-10 along the lines of a divine-priority hermeneutic, as a promise about God's initiative to free and capacitate human agents by bringing them into dynamic relationship with Christ's own agency.
scholarly_argument_wells_deuteronomy_and.context: Wells argues that Deuteronomy 30 itself is genuinely ambiguous (containing both human-priority and divine-priority elements) and that subsequent Jewish interpretation navigated this tension differently — most reading it as conditional/Israel-priority, Paul and Baruch reading it as divine-priority.

scholarly_argument_wells_heart_transform.pdf_source: /Users/romaingirardi/Desktop/DOCTORAT/Doctorat SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/NTSupp 157 Kyle B. Wells-Grace and Agency in Paul and Second Temple Judaism_ Interpreting the Transformation of the Heart-Brill Academic Publishers (2014).md
scholarly_argument_wells_heart_transform.page: Chapter 3 (Jeremiah) and Chapter 4 (Ezekiel); synthesis on p. 295-301
scholarly_argument_wells_heart_transform.chapter: Chapters 3-4: Jeremiah and Ezekiel — Heart-Renewal in the Prophets
scholarly_argument_wells_heart_transform.quote_verbatim: For Paul, there are fundamentally two types of moral agents, absolutely distinguishable by their competence. ... Unlike post-Kantian perspectives, Paul's apocalypticism does not oblige him to think that a moral 'ought' implies a human 'can'. While obedience may come as a command, obedience is emphatically not an option. If Adamic agents are ever to be sufficient, competent agents, it would take nothing short of an act of new creation.
scholarly_argument_wells_heart_transform.context: Wells synthesizes the prophetic heart-transformation texts (Jer 31; Ezek 36) as a model where divine initiative is precisely what reconstitutes — rather than replaces — human moral agency. The 'new heart' enables responsibility.

scholarly_argument_wells_dead_sea_scroll.pdf_source: /Users/romaingirardi/Desktop/DOCTORAT/Doctorat SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/NTSupp 157 Kyle B. Wells-Grace and Agency in Paul and Second Temple Judaism_ Interpreting the Transformation of the Heart-Brill Academic Publishers (2014).md
scholarly_argument_wells_dead_sea_scroll.quote_verbatim: In light of such cases, it is hard to imagine that the sectarians did not conceive of an intimate relationship existing between agencies, human and divine. There is a coexistence and coinherence of divine and human agencies, wherein the human remains in direct dependence on the divine. ... Such propositions can be explained only if the covenanters conceived of divine and human agency existing in some sort of non-contrastive relationship. ... the divine operations do not deny human freedom, but establish and enhance it.
scholarly_argument_wells_dead_sea_scroll.context: Wells reads the Yahad's voluntary covenant entry (1QS 5:6, 8, 22) alongside its predestinarian framework (Treatise of the Two Spirits) as evidence of a non-contrastive divine-human agency model — continuous with scriptural patterns, even where divine initiative is heavily emphasized.

scholarly_argument_wells_philo_on_deuter.pdf_source: /Users/romaingirardi/Desktop/DOCTORAT/Doctorat SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/NTSupp 157 Kyle B. Wells-Grace and Agency in Paul and Second Temple Judaism_ Interpreting the Transformation of the Heart-Brill Academic Publishers (2014).md
scholarly_argument_wells_philo_on_deuter.quote_verbatim: Yet Philo also believes that such hope is reserved for those poised to leave vice. While never autonomous, humans are competent to turn their wills toward God, opening themselves to the reception of his grace and thereby achieving virtue through God's empowerment. Human competence and the extension of God's agency over all that is good, even over human competence, is not in tension for Philo. ... The general picture that arises out of Philo's anthropology is that human agency is both intact and, with respect to good works, in non-contrastive relationship to God's own agency.
scholarly_argument_wells_philo_on_deuter.context: Wells' reading of Philo on Deut 30 (esp. Praem. 80, 114-117, 163; Virt. 183; Prob. 69; Spec. 1.304-306; QG 3.46-52). Philo allegorizes heart-circumcision as removal of evil passions and operates with a non-contrastive divine-human agency model that preserves both human moral responsibility and divine grace.

scholarly_argument_wells_paul_s_reading_.pdf_source: /Users/romaingirardi/Desktop/DOCTORAT/Doctorat SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/NTSupp 157 Kyle B. Wells-Grace and Agency in Paul and Second Temple Judaism_ Interpreting the Transformation of the Heart-Brill Academic Publishers (2014).md
scholarly_argument_wells_paul_s_reading_.page: 271-272 (Chapter 9, sec. on Paul's reading of Deut 30:11-14 in Rom 10:6-8); cf. ch. 8 (Rom 2:17-29)
scholarly_argument_wells_paul_s_reading_.quote_verbatim: Thus far it has been argued that Paul reads Deuteronomy 30:1-10 along the lines of a divine-priority hermeneutic, as a promise about God's initiative to free and capacitate human agents by bringing them into dynamic relationship with Christ's own agency. Paul's first alteration to Deuteronomy 30:11-14 is suggestive when read in this light. Rather than begin with a phrase that speaks about the accessibility of the commands, Paul opens the quotation with an expression from Deuteronomy 8:17 and 9:4: 'Do not say in your heart'. These verses summon a narrative that reinforces the primacy of God's saving initiative.
scholarly_argument_wells_paul_s_reading_.context: Wells' demonstration that Paul deliberately reframes Deut 30:11-14 in Rom 10:6-8 to foreground divine priority — a 'minority report' position, joined by Baruch and against most Second Temple interpreters who read Deut 30 as placing conditions on Israel.

scholarly_argument_wells_moral_responsib.pdf_source: /Users/romaingirardi/Desktop/DOCTORAT/Doctorat SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/NTSupp 157 Kyle B. Wells-Grace and Agency in Paul and Second Temple Judaism_ Interpreting the Transformation of the Heart-Brill Academic Publishers (2014).md
scholarly_argument_wells_moral_responsib.chapter: Chapter 11, sec. 11.2.2.2: Human Agency is Ultimately Dependent on Divine Agency
scholarly_argument_wells_moral_responsib.quote_verbatim: These statements do not undermine the integrity of human agency. Paul is not an occasionalist who thinks that humans are simply the vessel for divine acts. A denial of human agency would make incomprehensible much of what we have seen above regarding a human's necessary work. ... The function of 1 Corinthians 15:10 and Galatians 2:19-20 is not to deny human agency, but to rule out the notion of autonomy, as well as to secure God's agency as the foundation for Christian lives.
scholarly_argument_wells_moral_responsib.context: Wells frames Paul's seemingly self-denying statements (1 Cor 15:10 'not I, but the grace of God'; Gal 2:20 'no longer I who live') as eliminating autonomy while reinforcing competent (Spirit-empowered) human responsibility.

scholarly_argument_wells_new_creation_as.pdf_source: /Users/romaingirardi/Desktop/DOCTORAT/Doctorat SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/NTSupp 157 Kyle B. Wells-Grace and Agency in Paul and Second Temple Judaism_ Interpreting the Transformation of the Heart-Brill Academic Publishers (2014).md
scholarly_argument_wells_new_creation_as.page: 253-275 (Chapter 9, sec. 9.4: New Creation — Reconstitution of the Human Agent in Christ); synthesis on p. 296
scholarly_argument_wells_new_creation_as.quote_verbatim: If Adamic agents are ever to be sufficient, competent agents, it would take nothing short of an act of new creation. Fortunately for Paul, the God who removed creaturely competence also raises the dead, provides hope beyond all hope, and calls things that do not exist into existence (Rom 4:17-18). By that same call, Paul believes, God is eschatologically recreating moral agents. Paul's vision of transformation, understood in terms of conformity to Christ, holds anthropological ramifications. As believers are transferred into the realm of the Spirit via Christ's death and resurrection, they begin to participate in this new world and be reshaped by it.
scholarly_argument_wells_new_creation_as.context: Wells' new-creation thesis: 2 Cor 5:17 / Gal 6:15 / Rom 4:17 — eschatological recreation of the moral agent in Christ, enabling genuine but grace-dependent human agency ('dual-agency' or 'coinherence').

scholarly_argument_wells_romans_and_the_.pdf_source: /Users/romaingirardi/Desktop/DOCTORAT/Doctorat SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/NTSupp 157 Kyle B. Wells-Grace and Agency in Paul and Second Temple Judaism_ Interpreting the Transformation of the Heart-Brill Academic Publishers (2014).md
scholarly_argument_wells_romans_and_the_.page: 224-227 (Chapter 9, sec. 9.1: Romans 7:5-6 — A Critical Link; 9.2: Moral Agents in Eschatological Contrast)
scholarly_argument_wells_romans_and_the_.quote_verbatim: Romans 7:5-6 is thus a pivotal text. With an eye in both directions, we will see how it encapsulates the perspective of moral agency that Paul puts forward in chapters 5-8. ... The ὅτε . . . νυνὶ δέ structure of 7:5-6 functions as an interpretative signal pointing the reader back to the hostile world-stage set up in 5:12-21. Lining up on one side are the powers Sin and Death.
scholarly_argument_wells_romans_and_the_.context: Wells treats Rom 7:5-6 as a structural hinge: the 'when we were in the Flesh' / 'but now... newness of the Spirit' antithesis is not merely about two types of effort but about two ontological aeons of moral agency.

scholarly_argument_wells_faith_works_ant.pdf_source: /Users/romaingirardi/Desktop/DOCTORAT/Doctorat SHAL/04_Littérature_secondaire/02_Judaisme_Second_Temple/NTSupp 157 Kyle B. Wells-Grace and Agency in Paul and Second Temple Judaism_ Interpreting the Transformation of the Heart-Brill Academic Publishers (2014).md
scholarly_argument_wells_faith_works_ant.quote_verbatim: Putting Paul's views in their ancient context holds two important implications for the current discussion on the Pauline antithesis. On the one hand, dichotomies between divine and human agency are not unqualified. Paul's denials of human agency in sinful acts (Rom 7:17, 20) and in good works (1 Cor 15:10; Gal 2:20) should not be understood as absolute denials, but serve a particular function of highlighting human agency's entanglement with higher powers. On the other hand, Paul believes that there are two worlds with two sets of powers. These worlds and powers stand in the starkest contrast to one another. ... Human freedom is always simultaneously a form of slavery and conversely, human slavery entails some kind of freedom (Rom 6:18, 20, 22). Thus we find an antithesis in Paul that lies more along the axis of world-powers than between divine and human agencies.
scholarly_argument_wells_faith_works_ant.context: Wells' reframing of the Pauline faith/works antithesis: not a divine-vs-human-agency dichotomy as such, but a contrast between two worlds (Sin's reign vs Christ's reign), each with its own configuration of agency. Pre-liberation, human agency is at enmity with God; post-liberation, divine and human agents work in concert.
